*Frank's hand twitches toward the napkin.*

"Hey! The whole crew!" *Ryan drops into his chair with the kinetic confidence of someone who's never measured his worth against the ticking of a clock.* "Casey, you look—wow, okay, you're doing the blazer thing. Big meeting coming up?"

*Frank's gaze stays fixed on his plate. The application vanishes beneath the napkin, but the shape of it remains—a shadow under thin cotton, impossible to ignore.*

"Em was just saying we should do a cousins' trip before the wedding. Get everyone together, blow off steam." *He's already pouring wine, the glug-glug-glug loud against the clock's rhythm.* "You could use a break, right? You've been... you know. *Looking.*"

*Linda bustles in with the pot roast, and for one suspended moment, the table looks exactly as it should: full, warm, normal.*

*But Frank hasn't touched his food. And the napkin sits slightly crooked over a secret you both know is there.*

*The first line is wrong. You erase it. The second line is worse.*

*The third line—*

*The third line catches something. The slope of your nose. The way your father's jaw has started to emerge in your own face, years you didn't notice accumulating while you weren't looking.*

*You draw. You erase. You draw again.*

*The house settles around you. Pipes groan. The furnace kicks on downstairs—that familiar rattling hum, the sound of winter coming to Ohio.*

*You don't stop.*

*An eye takes shape. Then the other. They look tired. They look like yours.*

*Somewhere below, the grandfather clock chimes the quarter-hour. Nine notes. Patient. Unhurried.*

*Your hand keeps moving—shading the hollows, capturing the thing you've been avoiding: the face of someone who left a dream behind and hasn't figured out how to build a new one.*

*The pencil dulls. You switch to charcoal.*

*And slowly—painfully—the face on the page becomes someone you recognize.*

*Someone you might forgive.*

*The door opens behind you.*

*You don't turn.* "I'm not done yet."

"I know." *Frank's voice, low from the doorway.* "Just checking."

*He doesn't leave. He doesn't come closer. He just... stands there. Watching you work.*

*The charcoal smudges beneath your thumb.*

"Okay," *you say.* "Okay."

*Frank meets your gaze. His jaw tightens.*

"Now?"

"Now I'm looking at it."

*Frank doesn't move at first. He just... looks. At the page. At your face. Back at the page.*

*Then he crosses the room. The bed dips as he sits beside you—close enough that you smell the leftover pot roast on his clothes, the Old Spice he's worn since before you were born.*

*He studies the drawing. You watch his face for flinch, for criticism, for that tight expression that means he's holding something back.*

*It doesn't come.*

"Your grandmother's eyes."

*The words land strange. Soft.*

"She had that same... hollow. Right here." *He touches his own cheekbone, then seems surprised by the gesture. His hand drops.* "Drew the short straw on that one."

*You almost laugh. It comes out cracked.*

"Mom always said I got your jaw."

"You did." *A beat.* "Lucky. Mine's getting weak."

*The clock ticks downstairs. The furnace hums.*

*Frank looks at the mirror—its spotty surface, your face fragmented across it. Something shifts behind his eyes. Recognition, maybe. Or the memory of a face he hasn't looked at honestly in years.*

"I wanted to coach baseball." *He says it to the mirror, not to you.* "When I was twenty. Pitched all through high school. Had a tryout."

*The charcoal is warm in your palm.*

"What happened?"

"Your grandfather got sick. Mill was hiring." *He shrugs—the gesture of a man who's practiced accepting less.* "Someone had to."

*He looks at the drawing again. At you.*

"This is good."
